name: Clipperton Island

pin.note: Approximate centre of the atoll (about 10 deg 18 min N, 109 deg 13 min W)

territory: France (state-owned overseas island under the Minister of Overseas France)

creatures.iucn_status: Vulnerable (VU); FishBase cites a 2023 assessment, Wikipedia cites 2016
creatures.status_note: Clipperton is an Important Shark and Ray Area partly because it is a silvertip nursery. The Clipperton angelfish is endemic but was Near Threatened (2010), so it was not chosen.

facts.statement: Clipperton lies in the eastern Pacific at roughly 10 deg 18 min N, 109 deg 13 min W.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The nearest land is Socorro Island in Mexico's Revillagigedo group, about 945 km to the northwest.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The atoll is about 1,080 km southwest of mainland Mexico and about 2,390 km northwest of the Galapagos.
facts.evidence_note: Distances listed in the geography section.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Roughly 1,300 km separates Clipperton from the Mexican coast, and it is more than 6,000 km from Tahiti.
facts.source_title: Clipperton / Ile de la Passion - Geography
facts.evidence_note: Location paragraph of the geography page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton has a tropical oceanic climate with typical temperatures of 20-32 C, and peaks reported up to about 37.8 C.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Annual rainfall is reported as 3,000-5,000 mm, with relative humidity usually 85-95%.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The wet season runs from May to October, while December to March is drier; southeast trade winds prevail.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Storm season (May to October) brings strong swells and hurricanes, and the North Equatorial Current dominates January-May before the Counter Current takes over June-December.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Area description in the ISRA factsheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The island covers about 8.9 km2 including lagoon, and its emerged land ring is only about 1.7 km2 with an average height near 2 m.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The lagoon spans roughly 720 hectares, with deep basins of about 43-72 m, and has no fish.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The lagoon sealed off from the open sea roughly 170 years ago and is now stratified: oxygenated brackish water above and oxygen-free sulfurous water below around 15 m.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton Rock, the island's high point at 29 m on the southeast side, is made of trachyandesite and is about 100 m long.
facts.evidence_note: Height and geology sections of the rock article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton is the only emerged part of the East Pacific Rise, and the rock is the remnant of an extinct volcano's rim, hence the term near-atoll.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Fringing coral reefs surround the lagoon; reefs shallower than 20 m are dominated by Porites and branching Pocillopora, with large Porites, Pavona and Leptoseris at 20-70 m.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Area description in the ISRA factsheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Michel Dubocage reached the island on Good Friday, 3 April 1711 and named it Ile de la Passion; the English name comes from the pirate John Clipperton.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: France annexed Clipperton on 17 November 1858 as part of the Tahiti protectorate, and in 1892 a US claim under the Guano Islands Act was rejected.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Guano and phosphate extraction began in 1895 by a phosphate company, and Mexico removed American workers on 13 December 1897.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Mexico garrisoned the island from 1906, but resupply broke down during the Mexican Revolution and survivors (eleven people) were evacuated by USS Yorktown on 18 July 1917.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 1909 treaty sent the French-Mexican dispute to Victor Emmanuel III of Italy, who ruled for France in 1931; France took formal possession on 26 January 1935.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A US Navy weather station with 24 sailors operated on Clipperton from late 1944 until 21 October 1945.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton is uninhabited, and France administered it from French Polynesia until 2007, when it was placed under the Minister of Overseas France.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A bill adopted by France's National Assembly on 24 November 2016 gave the island its own legal status, direct state authority, and the alternative name La Passion-Clipperton.
facts.source_title: Proposition de loi n 150 (2016-2017) on the status of Clipperton
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Under that bill, landing or any activity on the island needs authorization, with penalties up to one year in prison and a 300,000 euro fine.
facts.source_title: Proposition de loi n 150 (2016-2017) on the status of Clipperton
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Fieldwork in 2005 estimated about 100,000 masked boobies (around 20,000 breeding pairs), described as the world's largest colony of the species.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The 2005 surveys also found about 7,000 brown boobies, fewer than 500 red-footed boobies, and over 1,300 great frigatebirds, whose first breeding on the atoll was recorded.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Bright orange land crabs (Johngarthia oceanica) swarm the island; pigs introduced in the 1890s suppressed them, and after the pigs were removed in 1958 the crabs recovered and cleared much vegetation.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The reefs hold more than 115 endemic species, including the Clipperton angelfish, Clipperton grouper and Clipperton damselfish.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2016 baited-video survey recorded Galapagos sharks on 83% of deployments and silvertip sharks on 33% at Clipperton.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Statements on sharks in the factsheet.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Black rats were absent in 1987 but spread across the island by 2003-2005, threatening ground-nesting seabirds; the authors called eradication urgent.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Industrial tuna fishing in the foraging area removes about 21,600 tonnes yearly, a risk for masked boobies that follow tuna schools.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Marine debris accumulates on the beaches, and a 2023 mission reportedly removed more than 200 kg of plastic waste.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: As of the 2009 report the authors stated that Clipperton had no legal protection status and urged rat eradication and tighter control of landings.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton is designated an Important Shark and Ray Area covering about 9.35 km2 from the surface to 100 m depth, based on silvertip and Galapagos shark nursery use.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The silvertip shark (Carcharhinus albimarginatus) is listed as Vulnerable and is a qualifying species for the Clipperton shark and ray area.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: In a 2005 expedition 29 silvertip sharks were sampled, mostly pregnant females with near-term embryos plus neonates, marking Clipperton as a nursery.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: Silvertips recorded in the 2016 survey averaged only about 65 cm fork length, and the survey authors judged most sharks of both species to be young-of-the-year.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: Tagged silvertip sharks have moved between Clipperton and the Galapagos, indicating regional connectivity.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: GBIF holds occurrence records of silvertip sharks at Clipperton, including 2005 specimens at the Paris natural history museum and a 2018 iNaturalist observation.
facts.source_title: GBIF occurrence search: Carcharhinus albimarginatus, France
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: FishBase lists the silvertip shark as Vulnerable (criteria A2bd), reaching about 300 cm total length and living from the surface down to 800 m.
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: Silvertip females carry litters of 1-11 pups after about a year of gestation, and the species is vulnerable to overfishing for fins and meat.
facts.subject: silvertip-shark

facts.statement: The Galapagos shark (Carcharhinus galapagensis) is a qualifying species of the Clipperton Important Shark and Ray Area and is listed as Least Concern (LC) in the factsheet; juveniles averaged about 82.3 cm fork length on 2016 baited cameras, against a length at birth of about 80 cm total length.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Species and survey tables of the ISRA factsheet. Status wording is the factsheet's own, not checked on the Red List site.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The oceanic whitetip shark is named as a supporting species of the Clipperton Important Shark and Ray Area and is listed as Critically Endangered (CR) by the IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group factsheet.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Supporting-species list in the ISRA factsheet; the page gives no Clipperton population figure for this species.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The scalloped hammerhead is listed as Critically Endangered (CR) in the Clipperton Important Shark and Ray Area factsheet, which names it among the species supporting the area's designation.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Supporting-species list in the ISRA factsheet; no abundance numbers given at Clipperton. Scientific name not given in the text read, so omitted.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The whale shark is listed as Endangered (EN), and the oceanic manta ray as Endangered (EN), among the supporting species recorded for the Clipperton Important Shark and Ray Area.
facts.publisher: IUCN SSC Shark Specialist Group (Important Shark and Ray Areas)
facts.evidence_note: Supporting-species list in the ISRA factsheet; the factsheet also lists shortfin mako (EN) and silky shark (VU). Scientific names not given in the text read, so omitted.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The Clipperton angelfish is endemic to Clipperton and is shown as Near Threatened in the IUCN categories cited by Wikipedia (2010 assessment), living at roughly 6 to 100 m depth.
facts.evidence_note: Status, range and depth on the species page; that page says little is known of its biology and gives no population estimate. Status is Wikipedia's citation of an IUCN assessment (2010), not read at IUCN. Scientific name not given in the text read, so omitted.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In 2005 the Nazca (Grant's) booby (Sula granti) was counted at fewer than 50 birds on Clipperton, with 10 to 15 breeding pairs near the coconut grove, including two pairs mixed with masked boobies.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.evidence_note: Seabird table in the Weimerskirch et al. chapter (counts January-March 2005). Read through a page summary tool; counts should be rechecked against the PDF.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The land crab Johngarthia oceanica, formally described in 2019 after being treated as a subspecies of J. planata, lives on Clipperton and on Socorro Island in Mexico's Revillagigedo Islands; the page gives no IUCN assessment for it.
facts.evidence_note: Taxonomy and range statements on the species page; absence of a Red List category is as stated by that page, not checked elsewhere.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Of 190 sponge specimens collected on three expeditions to Clipperton, 20 species were identified and nine of them were found only at Clipperton, including Callyspongia roosevelti.
facts.evidence_note: Wildlife/endemism section of the Wikipedia article.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In 2005 the surface layer of Clipperton's lagoon (0 to 10 m) averaged salinity of about 5.7, making it brackish, while the deep layer was near seawater at about 35.
facts.source_title: Biogeochimie du lagon (Charpy, Rodier, Sarazin), chapter 68 in Clipperton: environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique
facts.evidence_note: Salinity section, pp. 70-71 of the Charpy et al. chapter. Measurements from a few weeks of early-2005 fieldwork.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Below the brackish top layer, the deep water of Clipperton's lagoon was anoxic with an average pH of 6.8 and a strong hydrogen sulfide smell, while the surface layer was oxygenated with pH averaging 8.3 (2005 measurements).
facts.source_title: Biogeochimie du lagon (Charpy, Rodier, Sarazin), chapter 68 in Clipperton: environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique
facts.evidence_note: Oxygen and pH paragraph, pp. 70-71; a deep eastern-pit sample held about 3,785 micromol/L of H2S, but the page places the sampled depth inconsistently.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Water in the freshwater lens on Clipperton's land strip had a salinity of about 0.2 in 2005, but its nitrate and phosphate levels were far above French drinking-water norms, so the authors advised against drinking it and judged it suitable for washing.
facts.source_title: Biogeochimie du lagon (Charpy, Rodier, Sarazin), chapter 68 in Clipperton: environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique
facts.evidence_note: Freshwater lens paragraph, p. 77 of the Charpy et al. chapter.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: An early-2023 expedition found cold-water bleaching on Clipperton's deep reefs, with about 70 percent of the coral at 32 m recorded as bleached and dead after cold water was pushed to unusually shallow depths; the paper ties this to changes in easterly wind strength.
facts.source_title: Severe cold-water bleaching and mortality of deep-water reef observed in the Eastern Tropical Pacific
facts.evidence_note: Press release of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry (Oct 2024) on a paper in Science of the Total Environment vol. 951. Same page says surface water averages about 28 C for most of the year. Read via summary tool.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: During the 2018 Tara Pacific expedition, live coral cover on four shallow reef zones at Clipperton averaged 66 percent (range 55 to 85 percent), with massive Porites at 48 percent and branching Pocillopora at 15 percent.
facts.source_title: Springer article on Clipperton Atoll coral cover and pink-spotted phenotype (Tara Pacific 2018)
facts.evidence_note: Abstract page of the article; the same abstract notes a pink-spotted phenotype in about 27 percent of Porites and 31 percent of Pavona, possibly linked to past heatwaves or guano nutrients. Article title not captured from the page.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Coral surveys at Clipperton in 2005, 2016 and 2019 found overall cover of about 50-60%, with 44-56% variation in coral community attributes among years; live cover increased in 2019 after severe 2015-2016 El Niño heat stress and many tropical cyclones, with massive Porites replacing branching Pocillopora in shallow zones.
facts.source_title: Springer article on Clipperton Atoll coral community change 2005-2019
facts.evidence_note: Abstract page of the article. Overlaps the 2018 survey figure in this set but uses different years and methods; the two cover values differ and should not be merged. Article title not captured. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: In the southeast North Pacific, storms average at least six per year, about two reaching hurricane strength; a 1925 tabulation cited in the bulletin puts about 24 percent in October (September figure garbled in the scan, probably about 34 percent) and none from March to May.
facts.source_title: Atoll Research Bulletin No. 86: Geography and land ecology of Clipperton Island (Sachet)
facts.publisher: Smithsonian Institution Research Online (Pacific Science Board, NAS-NRC)
facts.evidence_note: Hurricanes section of Atoll Research Bulletin 86 (1962), citing Visher 1925. Historical, so not a modern climatology; it differs from the May-October storm season in the shark factsheet and the April-September cyclone season on Wikipedia. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Tropical cyclones affect Clipperton from April to September, though most pass northeast of the island; Hurricane Felicia in 1997 began in its path, Tropical Storm Andres struck in 2003 and Hurricane Sandra in 2015.
facts.evidence_note: Climate section of the Wikipedia article. Season months disagree with Sachet's bulletin, which puts the peak in September-October.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A U.S. Navy note records a hurricane at Clipperton on 12 October 1944 with winds estimated at 80 to 100 knots, and the bulletin adds that distant storms can raise waves high enough to flood the low land strip.
facts.source_title: Atoll Research Bulletin No. 86: Geography and land ecology of Clipperton Island (Sachet)
facts.publisher: Smithsonian Institution Research Online (Pacific Science Board, NAS-NRC)
facts.evidence_note: Hurricanes section of Atoll Research Bulletin 86; the account is credited to Taylor (1944). Wind speed is an estimate.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Clipperton sits on the edge of the Pacific dry zone, which, according to a note from the U.S. Weather Bureau in the Sachet bulletin, becomes rainier and shifts position roughly every decade during El Nino years.
facts.source_title: Atoll Research Bulletin No. 86: Geography and land ecology of Clipperton Island (Sachet)
facts.publisher: Smithsonian Institution Research Online (Pacific Science Board, NAS-NRC)
facts.evidence_note: El Nino paragraph of Atoll Research Bulletin 86 (1962); an older statement, not a modern ENSO analysis.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Between 11 August and 17 September 1958 a rain gauge on Clipperton collected 890 mm, with 125 to 150 mm falling in some 24-hour periods.
facts.source_title: Atoll Research Bulletin No. 86: Geography and land ecology of Clipperton Island (Sachet)
facts.publisher: Smithsonian Institution Research Online (Pacific Science Board, NAS-NRC)
facts.evidence_note: Rainfall section of Atoll Research Bulletin 86; a six-week wet-season sample, not an annual total.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The lowest part of Clipperton's land strip, on the northeast coast, rises only about 0.65 m above estimated mean high tide, and the bulletin says storms several hundred kilometres away can raise waves high enough to batter the island and flood the lower areas of the strip.
facts.source_title: Atoll Research Bulletin No. 86: Geography and land ecology of Clipperton Island (Sachet)
facts.publisher: Smithsonian Institution Research Online (Pacific Science Board, NAS-NRC)
facts.evidence_note: Elevation and flooding section of Atoll Research Bulletin 86 (1958 observations); in 1958 a stretch about 430 m long was overwashed. Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Masked booby numbers on Clipperton fell to about 150 birds by 1958 under introduced pigs and recovered to roughly 112,000 by 2006 after the pigs were removed.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.evidence_note: Conservation and history discussion in the Weimerskirch et al. chapter. Read through a page summary tool, so figures should be rechecked in the PDF.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Brown boobies on Clipperton were estimated at 25,500 in 1980 but only about 7,000 were counted in 2005, and no eggs or chicks were found during the 2005 visit.
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.evidence_note: Brown booby entry and discussion in the Weimerskirch et al. chapter; the 1980 estimate is credited to Taxit and Erhardt.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: On Clipperton the coconut grove is the main nesting area for red-footed boobies, with brown and Nazca boobies nesting on the ground in and around it, noddies roosting there, and about 100 frigatebirds also resting there (the main frigatebird roost is on the ground along the lagoon's southern edge).
facts.source_title: Seabird chapter in Clipperton, environnement et biodiversite d'un microcosme oceanique (Weimerskirch et al., 2009)
facts.publisher: NOAA Fisheries SWFSC repository (hosting MNHN/IRD publication)
facts.evidence_note: Habitat notes in the Weimerskirch et al. chapter (2005 survey). Statement corrected after an independent re-read of the source.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: The WWF ecoregion entry places Clipperton at the edge of the Eastern Pacific Barrier, which it calls the world's largest deepwater barrier to dispersal of marine shore organisms, and notes the closed lagoon has a strong halocline and high eutrophication.
facts.source_title: Eastern Pacific Ocean, southeast of Mexico (marine ecoregion entry)
facts.evidence_note: Page says its data are no longer updated. It states seagrass covers about 45 percent of the lagoon, whereas Wikipedia says seaweed; the difference is unresolved.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: Refuse seen on Clipperton in March 2012, mainly on the northeast shore and near Clipperton Rock, included plastic bottles and containers, and leftover debris also came from American (1944-45), French (1966-69) and 2008 occupations.
facts.evidence_note: Pollution section of the Wikipedia article; the same section says the rest of the island is fairly clean.
facts.subject: island

facts.statement: A 2016 French ministry draft order proposed a biotope protection zone in Clipperton's territorial waters, banning mooring, stranding, waste dumping and mineral extraction, and protecting sharks, manta rays, other fish, coral and marine reptiles that it describes as IUCN-threatened.
facts.source_title: Note de presentation du projet de texte (Clipperton biotope protection)
facts.publisher: Ministere de l'environnement, de l'energie et de la mer (France), public consultation
facts.evidence_note: Presentation note for a public consultation (20 October to 10 November 2016); the page is a draft, and whether it was adopted was not confirmed. Word-file converted locally to read.
facts.subject: island
